newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian president to revitalise Turkish ties.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian president to revitalise Turkish ties.

text.p: Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov leaves for Turkey on Monday, hoping to revitalise relations damaged by communist-era mistreatment of Bulgaria's ethnic Turks.

Stoyanov said he would ask his Turkish counterpart Suleyman Demirel to intercede with the Organisation of the Islamic Conference to remove Bulgaria's name from a list of countries which do not respect Moslems' rights.

Under former communist leader Todor Zhivkov, Bulgaria's 1.5 million ethnic Turks were forced to give up their Islamic names and religious traditions, leading to an exodus of more than 300,000 to Turkey in 1989.

"I will raise this point to President Suleyman Demirel so that...this part from the resolution of the Islamic Conference in Morocco will be dropped," Stoyanov told reporters on Wednesday on his return from Kuwait.

Ethnic Turks' religious and cultural rights were restored after Zhivkov's overthrow in 1989 and many of those who left for Turkey have returned. The ethnic Turks' Movement for Rights and Freedoms has deputies in parliament.

Stoyanov, making his first trip to a Balkan country since he took office in January, said he would ask Demirel to press for an OIC contact group to prepare a report on Moslems in Bulgaria ahead of December's OIC conference in Kuwait.
Presidency officials said that as Turkey had asked for Bulgaria to be blacklisted in 1989, it was Turkey which had to initiate Bulgaria's removal from the list.
Stoyanov raised the issue during his visit to Kuwait and won the support of the emirate's government.
Presidency officials said Stoyanov would sign cooperation accords on defence, tourism, ecology and nuclear security, and would propose a free trade agreement between the two countries.

He will also discuss a regional initiative to combat organised crime and drug trafficking, already raised with Romanian President Emil Constantinescu, who visited Bulgaria in April. Drugs pass through Turkey and Bulgaria on the so-called Balkan route to Western Europe.
Stoyanov will follow his visit to Turkey with a visit to Greece in early July.
Turkey's ambassador to Sofia, Mehmed Ali Irtemcelik, told Standart daily he believed the two countries could cooperate in joining the European Union and bringing Bulgaria into NATO.
"Turkey and Bulgaria are not competitors for the EU. Our joint efforts and mutual cooperation can only make both countries' way to the EU much shorter," he said.
"Turkey, which has been a NATO member for 45 years and believes that Bulgaria has really entered a new era, is a strong supporter of its bid to join the pact."
